hints: Look closely at which circled groups are attached directly to the central CH (the alpha carbon) and which are out on the side chain.
Remember what two groups must meet to make a peptide bond by condensation, and check which of 1, 2, 4, 5 fit that pair.
walkthrough:
**Spot the alpha groups and the side-chain groups**

Both molecules are amino acids, so each has one central carbon (the alpha carbon) with an amine and a carboxyl attached. On the left, those are 1 ($-NH_2$) and 2 ($-COOH$). On the right, those are 4 ($-NH_2$) and 5 ($-COOH$).

Groups 3 and 6 look like $-NH_2$, but they are part of an amide in the side chain ($-C=O$ with $-NH_2$), not free alpha-amino groups.

**Recall how a peptide bond forms**

A true peptide bond is always a condensation between the alpha-carboxyl of one amino acid and the alpha-amino of the other, releasing water:
$$-COOH + H_2N- \rightarrow -CONH- + H_2O$$

**Pick the correct alpha pair**

So we need one alpha $-COOH$ (either 2 or 5) plus one alpha $-NH_2$ (either 1 or 4). Of the choices given, only 1 (alpha amine of the first) and 5 (alpha carboxyl of the second) gives that correct pair.

options.A: Two amino groups cannot condense together to make a peptide bond, you need one amine and one carboxyl.
options.B: Group 1 is the alpha-amino of the first amino acid and 5 is the alpha-carboxyl of the second, the correct pair for a peptide bond by condensation.
options.C: Group 2 is an alpha-carboxyl, but 6 is a side-chain amide nitrogen, not a free alpha-amine, so no peptide bond can form there.
options.D: Group 3 is a side-chain amide, not an alpha-amine, so it cannot pair with the alpha-carboxyl 5 to form a backbone peptide bond.
